newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian Finance Ministry extending debt maturities.
newsitem.headline: Russian Finance Ministry extending debt maturities.

text.p: Russia's Finance Ministry is gradually restructuring its domestic debt by extending the maturities of GKO discount Treasury bills and OFZ interest-bearing government bonds in recent weeks.
The Finance Ministry intends to continue this policy, focusing on the issue of longer OFZ bonds, officials said.
But government securities dealers said investors, especially foreigners, preferred the fixed-rate T-bills to the variable coupon OFZ bonds, although they are happy to buy longer dates.

The weighted average maturity of all paper rose to 162.9 days on Friday from 145.5 in January, while the weighted average maturity of floating-rate OFZ bonds rose to 341.0 days from 310.1, Central Bank figures show.
As of April 18 the nominal value of outstanding OFZ bonds was 36.08 trillion roubles, out of a total government securiites market of 283.33 trillion, with the rest in GKOs.
"We've already been issuing paper on a basis of six months and longer for half a year," said Bella Zlatkis, director of the Finance Ministry's securities department.
"We're only issuing the short three-month bills to set a three-month rate. But we will lengthen the debt profile by issuing OFZ bonds running for 1-1/2 to three years," she said.
The Finance Ministry intends to cover half its domestic debt funding this year from paper with maturities of 1-1/2 to two years, Zlatkis told Reuters.

GKO T-bills are issued in different maturities up to 364 days. The Finance Ministry in recent months has lengthened the typical maturity to eight months from six, and in recent weeks has resumed the issue of one-year bills.
OFZ bonds are issued in maturities of 12, 18 and 24 months, and the authorities have also issued a small amount of three-year fixed-rate OFZ bonds, of which more are promised.
Dealers said Finance Ministry hopes of increasing the proportion of OFZ may run up against a widespread preference by investors for GKO bills.
OFZ bonds are subject to higher taxation than GKO bills. And more conservative investors prefer the predictable return on GKO bills to the floating-rate interest on OFZ bonds.

Of the seven OFZs now in circulation, two pay semi-annual interest and the rest pay quarterly coupons. But the interest paid on OFZ bonds, calculated on the basis of yields of current GKOs, can change sharply from one coupon to the next.
As a result, as far as Russian investors are concerned, only large banks with plenty of liquidity like to trade them, said a trader at International Moscow Bank.
Foreign investors prefer long GKO bills, said Alexei Rybnikov, head of capital markets at Yevrofinans.

"The one-year maturity is optimal for them and enables them to secure a significant yield and not worry about anything. Why buy OFZs, whose return can fall significantly after a change in interest rates?" he said.
But salesmen working with non-resident investors said interest in OFZs was growing.
"They're just not used to the peculiarities of the Russian market, and they've got to get a feel for it," said one saleman.
"Non-residents can work well with floating-rate instruments but in Russia they still prefer paper with fixed returns."
Sergei Koshelenko, head of foreign exchange at CS First Boston, said foreign interest in OFZ bonds would grow as the coupon period was lengthened.

"Paper with a maturity longer than one year must have a coupon and it would be better if it was fixed. There's a lot of interest now in one-year paper, because you can forget all the terms there," he said.

For many foreign investors the new three-year fixed-rate OFZ bonds will be attractive, even though their 20 percent annual coupon is below the current 28 percent average yield for tax-exempt paper, said Andrei Vetrov of Mosnarbank.
The fixed-rate OFZs mature in 1999, well after January 1, 1998, when remaining restrictions on foreign investment in government securities are due to be removed.
